title: Public inquiries: what they reveal and how to make them work
label: 4 November 2026 · Constitutional safeguards
summary: Two former inquiry chairs, Sir Brian Langstaff and Sir John Saunders, told the committee that public inquiries are essential to democratic accountability but have weak points: who decides to hold them, how they are run (too adversarial or too slow), and how recommendations are followed through. They discussed differences between inquiries, concerns about trust when officials mislead or records go missing, delays in compensation, and proposed practical changes — clearer controls on calling inquiries, better follow-up on recommendations, faster action on risks, safer organisational cultures, and better public engagement.

chapters.title: Why inquiries matter
chapters.takeaway: Public inquiries are important tools of democratic accountability but they work only if their findings are acted on.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Do public inquiries play a substantial constitutional role in a democracy?

turns.speaker: Sir Brian Langstaff
turns.text: Yes. Parliament holds the Government to account, but it can't investigate everything in detail. Inquiries answer big public questions and show whether the Executive failed, which is vital for public trust.

turns.speaker: Sir John Saunders
turns.text: I agree. My inquiry began as a coroner's inquest and because the Government wanted to withhold evidence under public interest immunity, a public inquiry became necessary to allow families and the public to see the truth.

chapters.title: Who decides whether an inquiry happens?
chapters.takeaway: Currently Ministers decide to set up inquiries, which can create a political tension over when and whether one is held.

turns.speaker: Sir John Saunders
turns.text: The Home Secretary has the power to order inquiries, and that can matter. In one case the Home Secretary initially refused a public inquiry; the courts pushed the issue back and a public inquiry followed.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Should that decision sit with the Home Secretary or elsewhere?

turns.speaker: Sir John Saunders
turns.text: I wondered whether a coroner could decide, subject to judicial review. But there's a democratic argument: Ministers are accountable to Parliament, so that matters.

turns.speaker: Sir Brian Langstaff
turns.text: I recommended a parliamentary-controlled system to decide when public concern justifies an inquiry. Leaving the decision solely to the minister whose department is involved risks conflicts of interest.

turns.speaker: Lord Jones of Penybont
turns.text: Is there any non-political mechanism to take that choice out of ministers' hands?

turns.speaker: Sir John Saunders
turns.text: Not easily; democratic pressures—Parliament, the Opposition, and public demand—are the usual checks. The process should remain accountable to Parliament.

chapters.title: How inquiries are run: scope, style and evidence
chapters.takeaway: Inquiries vary; scope must be set carefully and the adversarial, lawyer-led style can slow or distort inquiry work.

turns.speaker: Baroness Hamwee
turns.text: Should the Government give reasons for accepting or rejecting recommendations and should chairs stay involved to track progress?

turns.speaker: Sir John Saunders
turns.text: Yes on follow-up. Also, set the inquiry's scope sharply up front. We're too adversarial: long, repetitive questioning and many lawyers make inquiries slow and hostile.

turns.speaker: Sir Brian Langstaff
turns.text: In my inquiry we used counsel to the inquiry to ask most questions, which helped control repetition and preserve collaboration. But different inquiries need different styles.

turns.speaker: Lord Burnett of Maldon
turns.text: Do inquiries risk becoming 'hunting grounds' that force witnesses to be defensive?

turns.speaker: Sir John Saunders
turns.text: Absolutely. Lawyers naturally close off escape routes with long questioning. As chair you can cut through, but the adversarial approach can make people defensive and slow things down.

turns.speaker: Sir Brian Langstaff
turns.text: Some inquiries uncover wrongdoing and that will harm trust, but thorough public investigation can restore trust if it leads to effective change.

chapters.title: The implementation gap: recommendations and compensation
chapters.takeaway: Inquiries often end with accepted recommendations, but implementation is patchy and slow, which damages trust, especially for victims awaiting compensation.

turns.speaker: Lord Bichard
turns.text: Did you find things so bad they threatened constitutional democracy?

turns.speaker: Sir Brian Langstaff
turns.text: Yes. In the Infected Blood case people were misled, documents went missing or were destroyed, and official lines were repeated without proper foundation. That undermines trust.

turns.speaker: Baroness Laing of Elderslie
turns.text: Why were your recommendations accepted but compensation delayed?

turns.speaker: Sir Brian Langstaff
turns.text: It was a mix of practical and political delay. Setting up the compensation body and staffing it takes time, and priorities were set that pushed some payments far down the list. That slow start mattered because many claimants are terminally ill.

turns.speaker: Sir John Saunders
turns.text: I addressed implementation by holding a follow-up hearing a few months after my interim report to ask, 'Have you started?' That prompted activity, but the Home Office resisted that approach.

turns.speaker: Baroness Hamwee
turns.text: So should there be a standard follow-up mechanism in the law?

turns.speaker: Sir Brian Langstaff
turns.text: Yes. The Inquiries Act lacks a formal follow-up. I recommended Parliament should control a system to respond to public concern and track implementation of recommendations.

chapters.title: Restoring trust: safety culture, risk and communication
chapters.takeaway: To prevent repeat failures, public bodies must adopt a stronger safety culture, respond quickly to risks, involve affected people, and communicate clearly.

turns.speaker: Lord Waldegrave of North Hill
turns.text: How can we make accountability work day-to-day, and handle the gap between Ministers and technical experts?

turns.speaker: Sir Brian Langstaff
turns.text: We need a better approach to risk and patient safety. Where risk exists, act early rather than waiting for certainty. Managers must be accountable for how they respond to concerns.

turns.speaker: Sir Brian Langstaff
turns.text: Create a culture like aviation: everyone responsible for safety, with whistleblower protections and plural expert advice rather than deferring to one 'white coat'.

turns.speaker: Lord Griffiths of Burry Port
turns.text: What about communicating the inquiry's work to the public so they understand why it takes time?

turns.speaker: Sir John Saunders
turns.text: Keep communication open with victims and the public while preserving the inquiry's impartiality. The press can help hold authorities to account, but they can also misrepresent if they lack detail.

turns.speaker: Sir Brian Langstaff
turns.text: We ran an engagement team that met hundreds of affected people across the UK; keeping those most interested informed helps broader public understanding and builds trust.

turns.speaker: Lord Jones of Penybont
turns.text: To finish: is there any realistic way to remove the political element in starting inquiries?

turns.speaker: Sir Brian Langstaff
turns.text: Parliament must remain sovereign, but the mechanism for initiating inquiries should include parliamentary oversight so decisions are not left solely to the department involved.

turns.speaker: Sir John Saunders
turns.text: There's no perfect depoliticised route. The democratic process, pressure from Parliament, victims and the public is the practical check. We should focus on improving that process and follow-up.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you both. We've heard practical suggestions: clearer decision rules, sharper scopes, less adversarial hearings when possible, compulsory follow-up, quicker action on risk, and better engagement with victims and the public.
